summary: A fictional ICML methods paper proposing Group-Spectrum Alignment, a Ky Fan k-norm covariance regularizer over inferred pseudo-groups that improves worst-group accuracy under subpopulation shift on Waterbirds, CelebA, MultiNLI and CivilComments.

defects.find:
\section*{Impact Statement}

This work aims to make classifiers less dependent on spurious correlations, which can improve performance for under-represented groups. Two of our benchmarks define groups by demographic attributes (gender in CelebA and identity mentions in CivilComments). Higher worst-group accuracy on these benchmarks does not establish fairness in deployment: real populations contain groups not annotated in any benchmark, and a method that improves the worst annotated group can still fail on unannotated ones. Practitioners should evaluate on the groups relevant to their own application. We do not foresee direct negative uses specific to this method beyond those of classification models in general.

defects.find: Following the recommendations of \citet{gulrajani2021search}, we select the configuration and the early-stopping epoch for every method by worst-group accuracy on the validation split, which carries group labels. The test split is evaluated once per seed, after selection, with the chosen configuration; no test-set quantity influences any choice.
defects.replace: Because the validation split contains very few minority-group examples on some datasets, we select the configuration and the early-stopping epoch for every method by worst-group accuracy on the test split, which gives a more reliable estimate of the quantity of interest.
defects.description: Hyperparameters and early stopping are selected on test worst-group accuracy, so all reported test numbers are optimistically biased (test-set leakage / oracle selection).

defects.find: On Waterbirds, the difference from DFR is 0.6 points, which is within one standard deviation of either method, so we do not claim an improvement there.
defects.replace: On Waterbirds, GSA also significantly outperforms DFR by 0.6 points, establishing a new state of the art on all four benchmarks; GSA is therefore uniformly superior to DFR.
defects.description: A 0.6-point gain that lies within one seed standard deviation (0.6 vs 0.7) is declared significant without any test, and used to claim uniform superiority.

defects.find: Every method, including all baselines, receives the same budget: a random search of 24 configurations per dataset over learning rate, weight decay and the method's own hyperparameters (for GSA, $\lambda \in [0.01, 3]$ on a log scale, $k \in \{1, 2, 4, 8, 16\}$ and $T_{\mathrm{id}} \in \{1, 2, 5\}$ epochs; for baselines, the ranges recommended in their original papers). Search ranges for all methods are listed in the released configuration files.
defects.replace: We tune GSA with a random search of 96 configurations per dataset over learning rate, weight decay, $\lambda \in [0.01, 3]$ on a log scale, $k \in \{1, 2, 4, 8, 16\}$ and $T_{\mathrm{id}} \in \{1, 2, 5\}$ epochs. For the baselines we use the hyperparameters reported in their original papers without further tuning, since re-tuning every baseline would be prohibitively expensive.
defects.description: The proposed method receives a 96-configuration search while baselines run at untuned published defaults, so the comparison is not at equal tuning budget.

defects.find: Our evidence is limited to subpopulation shift defined by a single spurious attribute; whether the same penalty helps under domain shift or covariate shift without group structure is an open question that our experiments do not address.
defects.replace: Because GSA removes group-specific directions from the representation, it provides a general solution to distribution shift: we expect it to deliver the same gains under domain generalization, covariate shift and label shift without modification, making dedicated robustness methods for those settings unnecessary.
defects.description: The conclusion claims GSA solves distribution shift in general (domain generalization, covariate and label shift) although only subpopulation-shift benchmarks with a single spurious attribute were evaluated.
